participation.text: An elected majority governed within a constitutional settlement that protected opposition and made power subject to legal limits.

evidence.text: A voting photograph, an issued speech, procedural rules and the constitutional text answer different questions about the transition.

change.text: Election, constitution adoption, signing and commencement mark distinct changes; realization of rights requires further outcome evidence.

name: South Africa: making rights a constitutional commitment
geographicPrecision: Constitution-signing locality; a national political process extended far beyond this point.

interval.label: Democratic transition and final constitution, 1994–1997
interval.note: Selected transition:1996 signing and 1997 commencement are distinct. Not the end of every inequality or of the work of implementation.

question: What is the difference between promising a right and realizing it?
summary: Paul Weinberg’s photograph shows Nelson Mandela casting his ballot in the 1994 election. It records one person exercising a right in a transformed political system. The constitution-making that followed asked a further question: how could a government chosen by the majority be bound to protect dignity, equality and the rights of people who opposed it?

sections.title: The system being challenged
sections.text: Apartheid organized racial domination through law and administration. After the National Party came to power in 1948, it intensified an older history of segregation and exclusion. Restrictions on residence, movement and political participation shaped ordinary life as well as elections. Constitution Hill’s former prisons offer material evidence of that coercion: its history records incarceration and resistance, including anti-pass protests by women. A constitutional transition thus concerned much more than replacing the people at the top of government.

sections.title: Negotiation and an election
sections.text: Political organizing, resistance and negotiations preceded the 1994 election. Talks did not produce instant agreement: the process worked through competing demands and interim arrangements. An interim constitution supplied the framework for the election and a Government of National Unity. Mandela’s vote at Ohlange School in Inanda became an enduring image of the transition. It is one photographed act within a national election, not a picture of every voter’s experience or evidence that economic inequalities had ended.

citations.locator: Negotiations, interim constitution and Government of National Unity

sections.title: A majority needed constitutional limits
sections.text: Elected representatives also formed a Constitutional Assembly to write the new constitution. In May 1996 Mandela celebrated both majority government and constitutional protection for opposition. That pairing is central: winning an election should confer powers to govern, while leaving opponents able to organize and challenge the government. Public participation reached beyond those who could vote, including children. The speech describes the President’s view of this process; the precise protections must be read in the constitutional text itself.

sections.title: Adoption, review, signing and commencement
sections.text: The Assembly adopted a text on 8 May 1996, but adoption was not the final step. The Constitutional Court had to certify compliance with 34 principles inherited from the interim settlement. The text was amended in October after Court review. Mandela signed the constitution at Sharpeville on 10 December 1996, and it came into effect on 4 February 1997. These dates explain why the case spans 1994–1997. They should not be flattened into a single moment when all democratic institutions were complete.

sections.title: Read the rights carefully
sections.text: The Bill of Rights protects equality before the law and human dignity. Its political-rights section specifies rights of citizens, including voting rights of adult citizens. Other provisions use “everyone.” The wording and qualifications matter: access to adequate housing and health care involves reasonable measures and progressive realization within available resources, while the basic-education provision is worded differently. A list that reduces all of these to a promise of immediate identical provision would misstate the text.

sections.title: A commitment creates questions to investigate
sections.text: The constitution provides standards against which institutions can be challenged. It does not supply a measurement of whether a household obtained housing, a child reached school or an official acted fairly. Those outcomes need later records and people’s accounts. The transformation studied here ended apartheid rule and established a different constitutional order; it was not South Africa’s first independence from Britain. Compare it with Ghana and Indonesia by asking who could exercise and contest power, while retaining those different histories.

citations.locator: Sections 7–8 and 38, duties, application and enforcement

claims.text: The constitution was signed on 10 December 1996 and came into effect on 4 February 1997, after the 1994 democratic transition.

returnPrompt: Use one constitutional section to explain a commitment, then identify what evidence would test its effect in practice.

deeperReading.title: An invitation with a defined purpose
deeperReading.text: The Court’s May 1996 statement invited written objections to certification from people beyond the political parties. Objections could be in any official language, but had to identify a constitutional provision or omission and the principle it violated. The Court said its role was to assess compliance, not whether it considered the constitution wise. This was a particular avenue of participation with a defined legal question. It should not be confused with a general referendum on the whole text.

deeperReading.title: The practical conditions of participation
deeperReading.text: The same notice required a written objection of no more than 1,000 words, 25 copies and delivery by a stated deadline. These details make participation tangible: someone needed to compose, reproduce and deliver an argument. They suggest questions about access, literacy and assistance, but the notice alone does not measure who was excluded or how many people participated. Compare the procedural record with Mandela’s celebratory speech. One establishes the rules of an opportunity; the other presents a political interpretation of public involvement.

deeperReading.title: Read a famous photograph without making it carry everything
deeperReading.text: The photograph’s author and setting are known: Paul Weinberg, an official election photographer, recorded Mandela voting at Ohlange School near Durban. The image lets us inspect the ballot, box, people and room. It cannot show all the negotiations that enabled the vote, nor what happened after the shutter closed. A useful sequence therefore pairs the image with the interim settlement, the final constitution and later evidence about implementation. Political hope belongs to the history; claiming that the image proves every hope was fulfilled does not.

familyActivity.title: A right, a rule and a real result
steps: Describe the voting photograph without using the caption. Then identify what the caption adds.
Read the equality and education paraphrases below. Give an example of an institution each could affect.
Choose one example and name the evidence you would need to find out whether people actually benefited.
familyActivity.explanation: A commitment can matter greatly before every problem is solved. Distinguish the right, the institution responsible and the evidence of an outcome.

evidenceReading.title: Read who holds a right and how it is worded
evidenceReading.introduction: These are editorial paraphrases of the Bill of Rights, not quotations or a complete legal guide. Follow the section links and compare their wording.

items.label: Equality and dignity — paraphrase
items.text: Everyone is equal before the law and has inherent dignity that must be respected and protected.
items.interpretation: The subject is everyone. A historical inquiry can ask how institutions were required to change, then separately investigate their conduct.

items.label: Political participation — paraphrase
items.text: Citizens have political rights; every adult citizen has the right to vote in elections for a legislative body and to stand for public office.
items.interpretation: This provision specifies citizenship and adulthood for voting. Do not silently replace its wording with a claim that every resident had every political right.

items.label: Social rights — compare the wording
items.text: The text treats access to housing and health care, and the right to basic education, in separately worded provisions.
items.interpretation: Sections 26 and 27 expressly qualify state measures by resources and progressive realization. Section 29(1)(a) does not use that same formula. Reading the differences is part of understanding the promise.

review.scope: Bounded local teaching account; cited source passages and image records consulted.
limitations: This is a selected transition account, not a comprehensive history of apartheid, resistance, negotiating parties or political violence.
No independent assessment of rights implementation is claimed. The constitutional passages are read as historical commitments.
The 8 May 1996 speech is an issued text marked check against delivery, not verified audio or a transcript of the December signing.

placeStudy.title: South Africa: voting, drafting and signing in different places
placeStudy.description: Follow distinct actions across the country. The photograph was made near Durban, the Assembly worked in Cape Town, and the constitution was signed at Sharpeville. The line of argument is chronological; no travel route is drawn.

points.label: Inanda — the voting photograph
points.text: Paul Weinberg photographed Mandela casting his ballot at Ohlange School in April 1994. The image is evidence of this occasion, not the later signing ceremony.

points.label: Cape Town — constitution-making
points.text: The Constitutional Assembly worked in Cape Town. Mandela’s 8 May 1996 address celebrated adoption of the text and a mural marking public participation.

points.label: Sharpeville — signing
points.text: Mandela signed the constitution here on 10 December 1996. Signing preceded its commencement on 4 February 1997.

points.label: Braamfontein — the 1996 Court procedure
points.text: The certification notice identifies the Court’s then premises at Forum II, Braampark. The present Constitutional Court building at Constitution Hill opened in 2004; it should not be substituted for the venue in this 1996 document.
